_comment: Magnetic Effects WS1 (magnetic-1) - no printed key; answers DERIVED from physics.

_excluded_figures.desc: Two parallel conductors I and II positioned on a printed cm scale/ruler; zero-field point depends on the figure positions and current values (1 A, 3 A).
Graph options showing magnetic field strength B vs distance r from a current-carrying conductor; answer is one of four plotted graphs.
Diagram with axes U (vertical) and X-O-Y (horizontal) through point O with current out of the plane; asks which two points have mutually perpendicular magnetic field.
Rectangular loop ABCD carrying current I near a straight conductor XY (figure); asks how conductor XY moves.
Four diagram options showing the pattern of the magnetic field inside a current-carrying solenoid.
Straight wire with magnetic compasses placed at points X and Y as shown in the figure; needle deflection depends on figure positions.
Wire placed between magnetic poles as shown in the figure; direction of force depends on figure orientation.
Conducting wire between N and S poles (figure) with alternating current passing through; motion of wire depends on figure.
Uniform magnetic field in the plane of paper with an electron (e-) and a positron (p+) at marked positions in the diagram; asks the experienced force directions.

1.reason: Magnetic field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles.

2.reason: Force between parallel wires F proportional to I1*I2; doubling current in each gives 2*2 = 4F.

5.reason: Magnetic force is perpendicular to velocity, so speed and mass are unchanged; only the direction of velocity (hence momentum) changes.

6.reason: Field strength of a straight conductor depends on current, length of wire, and distance of the point.

7.reason: Direction of induced current in a conductor is given by Fleming's right hand rule.

8.reason: A fuse melts on excessive current, protecting against both overload and short circuit.

9.reason: Field inside a long straight solenoid is uniform - same at all interior points.

11.reason: Moving a magnet towards a coil changes flux, inducing a current (electromagnetic induction).

12.reason: By the right-hand thumb (grip) rule the thumb points in the direction of current; curled fingers give the field.

13.reason: Field inside a long current-carrying straight solenoid is uniform - same at all points.

14.reason: A transformer works on the principle of electromagnetic (mutual) induction.

15.reason: I = P/V = 4000/110 = 36.36 A. (Stem is garbled - the 4 A 'ranking' is a distractor.)

16.reason: REVIEW: Solenoid and A.C. generator/Cartesian system relate to right-hand rules; a D.C. motor uses Fleming's LEFT hand rule, so it is not an example of the right-hand thumb rule. Ambiguous - A.C. generator also uses Fleming's right hand, not the thumb rule.

18.reason: REVIEW: Same-length copper wires of different diameters: in series H proportional to R (more heat in thinner wire), parallel H proportional to 1/R; for a given supply over time t, total series resistance is higher giving lower current and less total heat, so H1 < H2. Stem partially garbled (text from a figure question leaked in source).

19.reason: Field at a point is directly proportional only to current (1); it is inversely proportional to distance and independent of conductor resistance, so 'Only A' (current).

20.reason: Many circular turns wound around an insulator form a solenoid.

21.reason: William Gilbert first established that the Earth itself behaves as a magnet.

22.reason: Inserting a soft-iron (ferromagnetic) core increases solenoid field strength.

23.reason: Field magnitude depends on number of turns, current, radius and core material, but NOT on the current direction (which only sets polarity).

24.reason: Alnico and Neodymium are standard permanent-magnet materials.

25.reason: Anticlockwise current (as viewed) corresponds to a North pole facing the viewer (clock-rule).

26.reason: Field inside a solenoid is uniform - same at all points.

27.reason: The tangent to a magnetic field line gives the direction of the magnetic field at that point.

28.reason: Field near a long straight wire forms concentric circles centred on the wire.

30.reason: Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction (not magnitude) of the induced current.

31.reason: Alnico = Aluminium, Nickel, Cobalt (Al, Ni, Co).

32.reason: Inside a solenoid the field lines are straight (i); around a straight conductor they are circular (ii).

33.reason: REVIEW: B = mu0*n*I = 4pi e-7 * (210/0.5) * 8 = 4.22 e-3 T = 422.4 e-5 T. Mantissa 422.4 matches option B, but its printed exponent (e-7) is a typo; closest intended answer is B.

34.reason: Positive charge moving west deflected north: F = qv x B with v=west, F=north requires B directed upward.

35.reason: A geyser is a high-power appliance; a 15 A fuse is used.

36.reason: A short circuit drops resistance to near zero, so current increases heavily.

37.reason: Beyond saturation, increasing current cannot increase magnetisation - the core/solenoid is magnetically saturated.

38.reason: Lighting/fan circuits (bulb, tube, fan) use a 5 A rating; 15 A is for high-power appliances.

43.reason: 15 A wiring is provided for high-power appliances such as a geyser.

44.reason: Field strength at a point is measured by the number of field lines crossing a unit area (lines crossing a given point).

46.reason: Electron (negative) moving up, B from south to north: v x B = west, so F = -e(v x B) = east; beam deflects towards east.

47.reason: Field lines inside a solenoid are parallel straight lines (uniform field).

48.reason: Oersted discovered that an electric current produces a magnetic field.

49.reason: Field inside a long straight current-carrying solenoid is uniform - same at all points.

50.reason: A fuse is the primary safety device protecting against short circuit and overload.
